title: Control variates and antithetics
objectives: Cut Monte Carlo error with antithetic draws and a control variate.

screens.title: Three estimators, one call
screens.prose: Three running means of our call, on a log axis of draws. **Plain** averages discounted payoffs. **Antithetic** averages each payoff with its mirror at $-z$. **Control** subtracts a multiple of the discounted share's surprise, whose mean we know. Watch the bands.

state.caption: Each band is the running mean ± 2 SE. All three share the same normal draws; the antithetic line pairs each $z$ with $-z$.

screens.question: Which band is narrowest after 10,000 draws?

options.why: Antithetic narrows the band, but less. Per draw its variance is a quarter of plain, from two payoffs; the control's is a seventh.
Plain is the widest band. The other two reuse what they know about the share.

One band hugs the line at £10.4506.

feedback.correct: The control's band is the narrowest.

explain.text: The control's band is about $\sqrt{6.9} = 2.6$ times narrower than the plain one. Antithetics help less. Both use the same draws, so the gap is the estimator, not luck.

screens.title: A control with a known mean
screens.prose: Let $Y$ be the discounted payoff and $X = e^{-rT}S_T$ the discounted share, whose mean is exactly $S_0 = 100$. The **control variate** estimator averages $Y - b(X - 100)$: still unbiased, for any fixed $b$. The table has the exact moments for our call.
screens.question: Which $b$ minimises $\text{Var}(Y - bX)$? It is $\text{Cov}(Y, X)/\text{Var}(X)$.

hints.text: Divide the covariance by the control's variance.
About 0.6736.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide $\text{Cov}(Y, X)$ by $\text{Var}(X)$.

byKey.inv: You divided the other way. $b^*$ is the covariance over the control's variance.
byKey.vy: You divided by $\text{Var}(Y)$. The control's own variance goes underneath.

explain.text: $274.91/408.11 = 0.6736$. It is the slope of a regression of $Y$ on $X$. From seed 0's paths it comes out as 0.67307.

screens.title: Why that b
screens.prose: Derive $b^*$ and what is left of the variance.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the one that does not belong.

lines.text: $\text{Var}(Y - bX) = \text{Var}(Y) - 2b\,\text{Cov}(Y, X) + b^2\text{Var}(X)$, since covariance is bilinear.
Setting it to 0 gives $b^* = \text{Cov}(Y, X)/\text{Var}(X)$, a minimum as $2\,\text{Var}(X) > 0$.
Take $b = 1$, because the call moves one for one with the share.
lines.why: You fixed $b$ by feel. At $b = 1$ the variance is $216.66 - 549.81 + 408.11 = 74.95$, more than twice the optimum 31.48.

hints.text: Start by expanding the variance of a difference.
A quadratic in $b$ is minimised where its derivative is 0.
Put $b^*$ back in, then write the result with $\rho$.

feedback.correct: The control removes the share of $\text{Var}(Y)$ that $X$ explains.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Expand, differentiate, solve, substitute.

byKey.d1: You set $b = 1$. The call moves about 0.64 per £1 of share at the money, so $b = 1$ over-corrects.

explain.text: The variance is a quadratic in $b$ with its minimum at $\text{Cov}/\text{Var}(X)$. What is left is $\text{Var}(Y)(1 - \rho^2)$, here $216.66 \times (1 - 0.92450^2) = 31.48$. The control removes the part of $Y$ that moves with $X$.

screens.title: The factor
screens.prose: For a fixed standard error, the paths needed scale with the variance per path. Plain Monte Carlo has $\text{Var}(Y)$; the control has $\text{Var}(Y)(1 - \rho^2)$.
screens.question: By what factor does the control cut the paths needed? Write it in terms of $\rho$.

hints.text: Divide the plain variance by the control's.
$\text{Var}(Y)$ over $\text{Var}(Y)(1 - \rho^2)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the ratio of the two variances.

byKey.nosq: You dropped the square. The residual variance has $1 - \rho^2$.
byKey.fraction: That is the share of variance left. The factor is its reciprocal.

explain.text: The ratio of variances is $\tfrac{1}{1 - \rho^2}$. It grows fast as $\rho \to 1$: 5.3 at $\rho = 0.9$ and 50 at $\rho = 0.99$. A control is worth having only if it is highly correlated.

screens.title: For our call
screens.prose: For our call and the discounted share, $\rho = 0.92450$. l15 needed 2.17 million plain paths for a standard error of £0.01.
screens.question: What is the variance-reduction factor?

hints.text: Square 0.92450 first.

byKey.rho2: That is $\rho^2$, the share of variance removed. The factor is $1/(1 - \rho^2)$.

explain.text: $1/(1 - 0.85471) = 6.88$. The same £0.01 then needs $2{,}166{,}609/6.88 \approx 315{,}000$ paths. The control is almost free: one more multiply per path.

screens.title: Antithetic pairs
screens.prose: Antithetics price each $z$ twice, at $z$ and $-z$, and average the pair. For our call the two payoffs in a pair have correlation $-0.501$. A pair average then has variance $\tfrac12\text{Var}(Y)(1 + \rho) = 54.06$. Two independent paths, the same cost, give $216.66/2 = 108.33$.
screens.question: How many times as efficient are the pairs, at equal cost?

hints.text: Efficiency at equal cost is the ratio of the variances.
About 2.0.

feedback.correct: Twice as efficient: the mirror cancels half the noise.

byKey.half: You divided the other way. The pairs have the smaller variance.
byKey.root: You compared standard errors. At equal cost, compare variances.

explain.text: $108.33/54.06 = 2.0$. Seed 0 with 50,000 pairs gives £10.4721 with SE £0.0329, counting pairs as the samples. Fit $b$ to the pair averages and both together leave a pair variance of 3.78.

screens.title: When pairs hurt
screens.prose: A straddle pays $|S_T - K|$ and is worth £16.0241. A colleague prices it with antithetic pairs, as he did the call.
screens.question: What do the pairs do for the straddle?

options.text: They make it worse: efficiency 0.61 against independent paths
They halve the variance, as for the call
options.why: You assumed pairs always help. Here the payoff rises on both sides of $K$, so $z$ and $-z$ pay alike.
You expected the correlation to vanish. It is $+0.645$, and a positive correlation hurts.

hints.text: What does the payoff do when $z$ is large and when $-z$ is large?
Both tails pay, so the pair moves together.
Compare 144.0 with 87.6.

feedback.correct: Antithetics are sure to help a payoff that is monotone in $z$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the pair variance with two independent payoffs.

byKey.better: You trusted pairs to help everything. They help only when the payoff moves in opposite ways at $z$ and $-z$.

explain.text: The pair correlation is $+0.645$, so a pair mean has variance $\tfrac12 \times 175.1 \times 1.645 = 144.0$. Two independent payoffs give 87.6, so the efficiency is $87.6/144.0 = 0.61$. The straddle rises on both sides, and its mirror draws agree.

screens.title: The Asian control in code
screens.prose: Price the arithmetic Asian call with the geometric Asian as control. The starter gives `geometric_asian_call`. Draw one row of 12 normals per path, all in one call, and build log prices by `np.cumsum`.

import math
import numpy as np
from statistics import NormalDist

def geometric_asian_call(S0, K, r, sigma, T, m):
    """Closed form: the log of the geometric mean of m equally spaced
    fixings is normal with this mean and variance."""
    t = np.arange(1, m + 1) * T / m
    mu = math.log(S0) + (r - sigma ** 2 / 2) * t.mean()
    v = sigma ** 2 / m ** 2 * np.minimum.outer(t, t).sum()

    d = (mu - math.log(K)) / math.sqrt(v)

widget.solution:
import math
import numpy as np
from statistics import NormalDist

def geometric_asian_call(S0, K, r, sigma, T, m):
    """Closed form: the log of the geometric mean of m equally spaced
    fixings is normal with this mean and variance."""
    t = np.arange(1, m + 1) * T / m
    mu = math.log(S0) + (r - sigma ** 2 / 2) * t.mean()
    v = sigma ** 2 / m ** 2 * np.minimum.outer(t, t).sum()
    N = NormalDist().cdf
    d = (mu - math.log(K)) / math.sqrt(v)
    return math.exp(-r * T) * (math.exp(mu + v / 2) * N(d + math.sqrt(v)) - K * N(d))

def asian_geometric_cv(S0, K, r, sigma, T, m, n, seed):
    """Arithmetic Asian call with the geometric Asian as control: (price, SE)."""
    z = np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal((n, m))   # one row a path
    dt = T / m
    logS = math.log(S0) + np.cumsum((r - sigma ** 2 / 2) * dt + sigma * math.sqrt(dt) * z, axis=1)
    y = math.exp(-r * T) * np.maximum(np.exp(logS).mean(axis=1) - K, 0.0)
    x = math.exp(-r * T) * np.maximum(np.exp(logS.mean(axis=1)) - K, 0.0)
    b = np.cov(y, x)[0, 1] / np.var(x, ddof=1)
    a = y - b * (x - geometric_asian_call(S0, K, r, sigma, T, m))
    return float(a.mean()), float(a.std(ddof=1) / math.sqrt(n))

screens.title: Machine time
screens.prose: An exotic desk needs a price to a fixed error. Plain paths take 10 hours on the grid of machines. The desk finds a control with a closed form and $\rho = 0.9995$, close to what the geometric Asian gives for the arithmetic one.
screens.question: How many seconds does the controlled run take for the same error?

hints.text: Find $1/(1 - \rho^2)$ first.
$1 - 0.9995^2 \approx 0.001$, so the factor is about 1,000.
10 hours is 36,000 seconds.

feedback.correct: About 36 seconds: a factor of 1,000 in variance is 1,000 in time.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 36,000 seconds by $1/(1 - \rho^2)$.

byKey.hours: You left the answer in hours. Convert 10 hours to seconds first.

explain.text: $1/(1 - 0.9995^2) = 1{,}000$, so 36,000 seconds become 36. Desks pick controls that have a closed form and track the payoff closely. The geometric Asian is the standard control for the arithmetic one; a European tracks the £90 down-and-out call less well, at $\rho$ of about 0.93 to 0.96.

ideas: A control $X$ with known mean gives $\overline{Y - b(X - E[X])}$; the best $b^* = \text{Cov}(Y, X)/\text{Var}(X)$ leaves $\text{Var}(Y)(1 - \rho^2)$.
The variance-reduction factor $1/(1 - \rho^2)$ is 6.88 for our call with the share. For the Asian with the geometric control it is about 1,300.
Antithetic pairs halve the call's variance, but hurt our at-the-money straddle, whose two mirror payoffs move together.

formula.name: Optimal control
formula.note: The control must have a known mean.

summary.trap: Antithetics do not always help: they are sure to help a payoff that moves one way with $z$, but for our at-the-money straddle they increase the variance.

quiz.question: What is the variance-reduction factor?

explain.text: $1/(1 - 0.81) = 5.26$: the same error from a fifth of the paths.

quiz.prose: A colleague uses the call's own payoff $Y$ as its control. Then $\rho = 1$ and the controlled variance is 0.
quiz.question: Why is this useless?

options.text: A control needs a known mean, and $E[Y]$ is the unknown price
A variance of 0 is impossible, so the code is wrong
options.why: You doubted the algebra. $Y - (Y - E[Y])$ really is constant; the trouble is that we do not know $E[Y]$.

options.text: It is biased because $b$ comes from the paths
options.why: You blamed the estimated $b$. That bias is tiny; the missing known mean is fatal.

feedback.correct: The estimator needs $E[Y]$, which is what we want.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write out $Y - b(Y - E[Y])$ with $b = 1$.

explain.text: With $b = 1$ the estimator is $E[Y]$ itself. To compute it we must already know the price. A control is useful only when its mean is known in closed form.

quiz.prose: A put is priced with the discounted share as control.
quiz.question: What sign does $b^*$ have?

options.text: Negative: the put pays more when the share falls

options.why: You carried over the call. The put moves against the share, so the covariance is negative.

options.text: Zero: a put and the share are unrelated
options.why: You expected no link. The put's payoff falls as $S_T$ rises.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how the put's payoff moves with $S_T$.

explain.text: The put's payoff falls as $S_T$ rises, so $\text{Cov}(Y, X) < 0$ and $b^* < 0$. For the half-year 95 put of l17 the paths give $\hat b = -0.292$. The control works the same way, with the sign flipped.
